lessons.title: What is a deepfake, and what is not?
lessons.subtitle: Not every generated image is one

sections.title: Three cases, not the same thing
sections.content:
Three cases. All three are invented, none describes a real event:

1. A manipulated video puts words in a known person's mouth she never said.
2. A fraud call uses a cloned voice and demands a transfer under time pressure.
3. An account builds trust with a generated profile picture and an invented biography.

The same check for all three? No. Cases one and two can be deepfakes in law, because an existing person or event is deceptively reproduced. The invented face in case three is synthetic content, not automatically a deepfake under the AI Regulation, as long as it resembles no existing person or entity.

And in none of them does appearance or sound prove anything. Neither authenticity nor manipulation.
sections.keyTakeaway: Deepfake and synthetic content are not synonyms. The question is whether existing people, objects, places, entities or events are deceptively reproduced.

sections.title: What the law calls a deepfake
sections.content:
The word has a legal definition, narrower than everyday use. Article 3(60) of the AI Regulation calls a deepfake AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing people, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful.

Different techniques sit behind it. Face swapping, lip synchronisation, speech synthesis, voice cloning, generative image and video models. How much reference material, at what quality, depends on the technique. No fixed number of images or minutes of audio exists.

The definition describes the result and its deceptive effect, not one model technique. Conventional editing can deceive too. It falls under this AI Act definition only when the content is AI-generated or AI-manipulated.
sections.keyTakeaway: The AI Regulation defines deepfakes through three marks: AI generation or manipulation, resemblance to something existing, a false impression of authenticity.

sections.title: Two duties since August 2026, and no proof of authenticity
sections.content:
Article 50 asks two different things of two different roles:

- Providers of covered generative systems must, as a general rule, mark synthetic output in machine-readable form as artificially generated or manipulated.
- Deployers who generate or manipulate a deepfake and disclose it must, as a general rule, state visibly that the content was artificially generated or manipulated. Evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous works get an adapted disclosure; further statutory exceptions have to be assessed.

Article 50 has applied since 2 August 2026. Providers of systems already on the market before that date must meet Article 50(2) from 2 December 2026 under the transition in Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. A marking can support provenance. Its absence proves nothing about authenticity. Not before that date, not after, because markings can be removed and exceptions can apply.

Sources: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 3(60) and Article 50; Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, Article 1(39)(b).
sections.keyTakeaway: Article 50 separates machine-readable marking by providers from visible disclosure by deployers. Both depend on context, and neither proves authenticity.

quiz.questionText: Which statement matches the AI Regulation's deepfake definition?

answerOptions.text: Every fully generated image is a deepfake, whatever its subject
Only content about public figures can be a deepfake
The term always requires particular software and a fixed amount of training data
The content is AI-generated or manipulated, resembles something existing, and would falsely appear authentic or truthful

quiz.explanation: Article 3(60) needs three things at once: AI generation or manipulation, resemblance to existing people, objects, places, entities or events, and a false impression of authenticity or truth.

quiz.questionText: Which technical statement about deepfakes is correct?

answerOptions.text: Deepfakes arise only through manual face swapping
Face swapping, lip synchronisation, speech synthesis and generative models can be involved
Every deepfake requires thousands of reference images
Only state actors can run the necessary techniques

quiz.explanation: Deepfakes are made with very different techniques. How much reference data and handwork it takes changes from technique to technique. No universal minimum exists.

quiz.questionText: Since when has Article 50 of the AI Regulation applied?

answerOptions.text: From 2 February 2025
From 2 August 2026
From 1 January 2027
The marking duty has applied since 2020 under the GDPR

quiz.explanation: Article 50 has applied since 2 August 2026. Providers of covered systems mark in machine-readable form under paragraph 2; deployers disclose deepfakes visibly under paragraph 4, as a general rule. For generative systems on the market before that date, the paragraph 2 transition runs to 2 December 2026.

lessons.title: How to check provenance and context
lessons.subtitle: Source work, not a detector verdict

sections.title: Tools for provenance, not for truth
sections.content:
No tool tells you whether an image is true. Three tool classes tell you where it came from:

1. Reverse image search: Google Lens and TinEye (tineye.com) can show earlier or similar appearances. An early hit points to context, not to the original source.
2. Video decomposition: InVID/WeVerify (weverify.eu) splits videos into keyframes, triggers reverse searches and shows available metadata. A research tool. Whether a video is true, it does not decide.
3. Provenance data: Content Credentials or other signed provenance information can document editing steps and issuers. Missing provenance proves no manipulation. Where it exists, check validity and issuer.

And before you upload: confidential, intimate or personal content does not go to a third party unchecked. Check data protection, terms of use and local alternatives first.
sections.keyTakeaway: Reverse search, keyframes and provenance data give signals. None of these tools decides authenticity or meaning alone.

sections.title: Five steps before you believe anything
sections.content:
1. Pin the claim: what should the content prove, when and where was it supposedly made?
2. Open the source: the earliest reachable post, the complete video, the account or outlet behind it. A screenshot without a link is no source.
3. Cross-check context: date, place, language, weather, visible signs and the uncut sequence against independent sources.
4. Look for provenance: use reverse image search or keyframes. Compare concrete image details, not just similar motifs.
5. Bound the result: write down what is confirmed, disproved, still open. "Not verified" is a permissible result.

Hands, hair, blinking, light, compression artefacts. Such oddities may make you look harder. A checklist they are not. Generators change, and the same oddities come from camera, cut or compression.
sections.keyTakeaway: Start with claim, source and context. Visual artefacts are signals, neither necessary nor sufficient to prove a deepfake.

sections.title: What a detector's percentage means
sections.content:
The detector shows a percentage. What you see is a model-dependent estimate. How much it is worth depends on training data, tested generators, compression, crop, post-processing and threshold. That number is not automatically a calibrated probability for your case.

Two limits follow:
- A negative result establishes no authenticity. The content can sit outside the known test distribution, or be altered.
- A positive result establishes no manipulation. Genuine recordings can trigger features the model misreads.

Use a detector as an extra signal at most. Anyone who wants to publish, accuse or litigate needs traceable provenance, context, further evidence and, where necessary, specialist forensic analysis.
sections.keyTakeaway: A detector score is a signal under known test conditions. It proves no authenticity, and alone no manipulation.

quiz.questionText: What can a reverse image search actually contribute?

answerOptions.text: Proof that an image was generated with AI
Automatic confirmation of all EXIF metadata
Earlier or similar appearances, and with them clues about context
Reliable identification of every person shown

quiz.explanation: A reverse search finds indexed identical or similar images. That can show earlier use or a different context. The earliest hit is still not necessarily the original source.

quiz.questionText: What beats a list of visual artefacts?

answerOptions.text: Counting fingers in a single frame
Treating poor image quality as proof of manipulation
Treating a missing watermark as proof of authenticity
Checking source, full context, earlier appearances and independent confirmation

quiz.explanation: Visual oddities move with every generator generation and show up in genuine, compressed or edited footage too. Source and context give evidence others can check.

quiz.questionText: What does a negative detector result mean?

answerOptions.text: The image is certainly genuine
A real person took the image
Under this detector's conditions no sufficient signal was found; authenticity is not established
The tool could not process the image

quiz.explanation: A negative result holds for exactly one model, one threshold and the content tested. An unknown technique or some post-processing, and detection looks different.

lessons.title: What to do when you find a deepfake
lessons.subtitle: Preserve, report, protect. Do not share.

sections.title: Five steps, and none of them is sharing
sections.content:
1. Do not spread it: no sharing, quoting or public comment. Not with a warning either. Where safe, preserve URL, account name, timestamp and a screenshot locally.
2. Check first, accuse later: a suspicion is no finding. Use the source check from Lesson 2.
3. Report precisely: use the platform's current reporting route, name the URL and the possible legal or policy breach. Article 16 of the Digital Services Act obliges hosting services to offer an easily accessible electronic notice mechanism for allegedly illegal content. Sufficiently precise notices have to be handled and decided in a timely, diligent, objective and non-arbitrary way. No duty to remove every reported item follows from that.
4. Tell the affected person privately: source location and evidence, without passing on the content.
5. On a possible crime or immediate danger, bring in the police: the competent online police station is reachable through polizei.de. In an acute emergency, call the emergency number.
sections.keyTakeaway: Do not amplify, preserve evidence, report precisely, protect the affected. A notice triggers a review and a decision. Not automatic removal.

sections.title: Three procedures, three recipients
sections.content:
Who breached what? That decides where your complaint goes. Article 50 separates machine-readable marking by providers of covered generative systems from visible disclosure by deployers who generate or manipulate deepfakes and disclose them. Exceptions and transition rules you check per role. For systems already on the market before 2 August 2026, Article 50(2) applies from 2 December 2026 under Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.

Article 85 lets you complain to the competent market surveillance authority. Under the KI-MIG that is generally the Bundesnetzagentur, as market surveillance authority, single point of contact and complaints body, unless a sector authority is competent. What counts is the officially published channel, not the address from an old blog post.

Platform notice under the DSA, criminal complaint, AI Act complaint: three procedures, three recipients, three sets of conditions.

Sources: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Articles 50 and 85; Regulation (EU) 2026/1744; KI-MIG.
sections.keyTakeaway: Platform notice, criminal complaint and AI Act complaint have different conditions and recipients. Check role, exception and current channel separately.

sections.title: When your image or voice is hit
sections.content:
Your face in a video you never shot. The basic rule is Section 22 KUG: portraits may be distributed or publicly displayed only with the consent of the person shown. The exceptions in Section 23 KUG and the balancing under Section 23(2) still apply. Whether a deepfake infringes them, and what claim follows, depends on content, context and distribution route.

Section 22 KUG does not protect your voice alone. With cloned or manipulated audio, the general right of personality, data protection law and civil or criminal provisions can apply, depending on use. Nobody can promise a particular legal consequence without seeing your case.

Preserve source location and evidence, without passing the content on. verbraucherzentrale.de and klicksafe.de give a first orientation. For your actual claims you need qualified media-law advice.
sections.keyTakeaway: Section 22 KUG holds the basic rule for portraits, Section 23 the exceptions. Voice, claim and route you check separately.

quiz.questionText: What do you do first when you hit a suspected deepfake?

answerOptions.text: Forward the video to every media outlet you know for analysis
Do not share publicly; preserve the source location and available evidence locally
Call the Federal Criminal Police Office immediately
Post your own fact-check on social media

quiz.explanation: Every public pass-along grows the reach, including the well-meant kind. Preserve URL, account, time and a screenshot where safe, then take the right reporting or authority route.

quiz.questionText: How do you find the complaint route for a possible Article 50 breach?

answerOptions.text: Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA)
Federal Financial Supervisory Authority (BaFin)
Always write straight to the Bundesnetzagentur, whatever the sector and published competence
Check official Bundesnetzagentur information, possible sector competence and the currently published authority channel

quiz.explanation: Under the KI-MIG the Bundesnetzagentur is generally competent, unless a sector authority is. So check the current official competence information and the published channel first.

answerOptions.text: The right to publish your own works of art
The photographer's copyright in their pictures
The basic rule that portraits may be distributed or publicly shown only with consent; statutory exceptions still need checking
The right to delete AI-generated images

quiz.explanation: Section 22 KUG holds the consent rule for distributing and publicly displaying portraits. Section 23 KUG holds the exceptions and a balancing of interests. Whether a deepfake infringes a right is decided case by case.
